name: Maine
summary_text: Maine is a comparatively low-risk state for a transgender visitor within the United States. A July 2026 national anti-trans legal risk assessment places Maine in its Low-Risk States group. The sources reviewed attribute to Maine none of the state-level document restrictions, facility bans or care bans documented elsewhere: no state law blocking marker changes, no state bathroom restriction and no state ban on gender-affirming care is recorded against Maine in this inventory.  The federal layer nevertheless governs a visitor in Maine in full. Under Executive Order 14168 of January 2025, federal identity documents must reflect sex assigned at birth; the State Department has stopped processing the X marker, new passport applications are decided as M or F on supporting documents, and passports already issued with an X remain valid only until expiry. The Supreme Court allowed those restrictions to take effect in November 2025. Screening at US checkpoints can require secondary screening, devices and pat-downs that out a traveller, and visa applicants who list a gender other than their assigned sex risk refusal as fraud, with a February 2025 ban on trans athletes entering to compete in women's sport.  Maine's favourable state posture does not insulate institutions from federal enforcement. In March 2025 the University of Maine System announced compliance with federal restrictions on transgender sports participation after the US Department of Agriculture suspended federal funding for research and programmes while investigating possible sex-based discrimination in federally funded education programmes. The July 2026 assessment separately flags Maine's risk as increased on that basis, the only factor cited against the state.  Maine Corrections houses transgender prisoners by current gender identity. Andrea Balcer, a 27-year-old transgender woman convicted of two murders, was being held in the women's facility at the Maine Correctional Center in Windham for at least a year as of April 2026. On 3 April 2026 another inmate, Katie Mountain, 41, filed a 30-page complaint in state court against Maine Department of Corrections Commissioner Randall Liberty, Warden Ben Beal and Balcer, alleging chronic harassment and assault by the transgender prisoner. Attorney Cynthia Dill filed the complaint. The placement is documented; the harassment and assault claims are allegations, and no ruling has been reported.  Federal custody and care policies apply within the state's federal facilities and to federally funded providers. The Federal Bureau of Prisons adopted conversion-therapy-style policies for transgender inmates from 2026 and stopped reporting the number of transgender prisoners held in 2025; the Department of Justice subpoenaed records of patients under 19 from more than 20 hospitals in summer 2025; and October 2025 proposed rules would bar Medicaid reimbursement for care to transgender patients under 18. Several of these federal measures have been blocked or enjoined in court, with the outcome of individual cases unresolved.

name: Maryland
summary_text: Maryland stands under United States federal law on identity documents, and that layer is the sharpest document risk for a trans visitor. Executive Order 14168 of 20 January 2025 defines sex for federal purposes as a male-female binary and requires federal identity documents to reflect sex assigned at birth. The State Department stopped processing the X marker and any marker inconsistent with sex assigned at birth, so new passports are issued as M or F on the supporting documents submitted, while passports already carrying an X remain valid until expiry. The Supreme Court allowed those restrictions to take effect in November 2025, superseding a State Department policy in force since 1992. Trans and nonbinary travellers report passports confiscated or blocked at application, with some left stranded abroad, and the ACLU is in litigation with the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs. No Maryland instrument can alter a federal passport, so a visitor's document may fail to match their presentation for the duration of the trip.  Entry screening adds a separate exposure. In February 2025 the State Department announced that trans athletes entering to compete in women's sports would be refused, flagging visa applicants with an internal marking, and treating an applicant who lists a gender other than their assigned sex as grounds for a permanent ban for fraud. Several foreign governments responded: in April 2025 multiple countries issued advisories about trans people travelling to the United States over identity-document and data rules, and in March 2025 at least eight countries, among them Finland and Denmark, adjusted entry guidance for trans and nonbinary citizens. Inside Maryland, travellers still pass federal checkpoint procedures under which secondary screening, devices and pat-downs can be initiated, an outcome that outs a passenger to officers in public view.  Facilities rules are restrictive at the federal layer. The same executive order barred transgender people from government-funded single-sex facilities congruent with their gender identity, which reaches federally funded settings in Maryland such as national park and federal building restrooms. The wider national tally is uneven: a Movement Advancement Project count records state bathroom bans applying to trans people in K-12 schools and some government buildings in nine states and one territory, outright state bans on facility use by gender identity in additional states, and no such ban in 29 states, four territories and the District of Columbia, with some states making trans bathroom use a criminal offence in defined circumstances. In April 2025 a transgender student was arrested and handcuffed in a women's restroom at the Florida state capitol, which civil-rights attorneys described as the first known arrest under that state's law.  Protective state law in Maryland has not removed documented violence against trans residents. On 11 September 2026 Sophie Lee, a 27-year-old Black trans woman, was found shot in Baltimore's Charles Village and died; it was the second killing of a Black trans woman shot to death in Baltimore within ten weeks. A July 2026 analysis plotting recorded anti-trans incidents against each state's law score placed Maryland in the 'Safest States' band with a law score of 23.5 and 11.1 recorded incidents, while Louisiana recorded the worst law score at 24.7 and the highest incident count at 11.6. The finding that a strong statutory floor does not by itself predict incident counts applies directly to how a visitor should read Maryland's reputation.  Detention carries documented harm under rules Maryland does not set. Federal policy on housing transgender prisoners moved in both directions between 2015 and 2018: a January 2015 immigration-detention memo directed that transgender detainees be housed according to gender identity, and 2016 Department of Justice guidelines forbade corrections agencies from assigning trans inmates to men's or women's units solely on birth anatomy, but the 2018 revision of the Federal Bureau of Prisons Transgender Offender Manual removed the commitment to recommend housing by gender identity and replaced it with case-by-case placement in which 'biological sex' is the initial determination and gender identity is used only in rare cases. From 2026 the Bureau adopted policies mandating conversion-therapy-style treatment for transgender inmates, including cutting hair short, withdrawing hormone medication and substituting psychiatric therapy and drugs, and it stopped reporting the number of transgender prisoners held from 2025. Trans women held in men's facilities are subjected to what sources describe as V-coding, the assignment of trans women to aggressive cisgender male cellmates, characterised as a central part of a trans woman's sentence, and trans women who physically resist sexual assault are often charged with assault and placed in solitary confinement, with the charge used to extend the sentence and deny parole. A 2021 California study found 69% of surveyed trans women prisoners reported unwanted sexual acts, 58.5% reported violent sexual assault and 88% reported a marriage-like relationship. A visitor held in Maryland stands under these federal practices.

sources.title: Fairness for All Marylanders Act of 2014
sources.documents: Statewide anti-discrimination protection based on gender identity; added gender identity to Maryland anti-discrimination law (sexual orientation protected since 2001).
sources.detail: No URL visible in text. Cited as: introduced Jan 2013, passed Senate 32-15 on March 4 2014, House 82-57 on March 27 2014, signed May 15 2014 by Gov. Martin O'Malley, effective Oct 1 2014; referendum petition failed.
